tool.excerpt: Usually this western negative is used, but the easternized keshikaranai → keshikaranē (怪しからない; rather than *keshiku nai/nē) has also been reported as an Edoism. === Negative: Grammatical compatibility === The eastern negative ‑nai generally works like an adjective, although its gerund ‑nai de is more common than the adjectival ‑nakute. The western gerund is ‑n(u) de. The imperfect negative can be followed by the noun uchi (内; 'interval; within'), whereby it means "while it hasn't happened" or "before it happens." Contradictorily, when it is followed by the nouns mae (前; 'front; before') and saki (先; 'tip; first'), it can also mean the same thing, even though the literal meaning would suggest "before it doesn't happen." Thus, konai uchi (来ないうち; 'before one comes') would mean the same as konai mae/saki (来ない前・先), and roughly as the affirmative kuru mae (来る前) which, however, may be used when the speaker has positive conviction that one will in fact come. The classical, and thus more literary than colloquial, ‑zu is originally the infinitive of ‑n(u), but it is often used conclusively with a copula. ... Japanese conjugation, like the conjugation of verbs of many other languages, allows verbs to be morphologically modified to change their meaning or grammatical function. In Japanese, the beginning of a word (the stem) is preserved during conjugation, while the ending of the word is altered in some way to change the meaning (this is the inflectional suffix). tool.title: Food security
tool.excerpt: Food security is the state of having reliable access to a sufficient quantity of affordable, healthy food. The availability of food for people of any class, gender, status, ethnicity, or religion is another element of food protection. Similarly, household food security is considered to exist when all the members of a family have consistent access to enough food for an active, healthy life. Food-secure individuals do not live in hunger or fear of starvation. Food security includes resilience to future disruptions of food supply. Such a disruption could occur due to various risk factors such as droughts and floods, shipping disruptions, fuel shortages, economic instability, and wars. Food insecurity is the opposite of food security: a state where there is only limited or uncertain availability of suitable food.
